questions.text: After 10+ years in sales, how have you changed the way you communicate with prospects — what do you do now that you didn't do early in your career?

answers.text: I communicate more clearly and professionally than I used to. I've picked up a lot of skills over the years that help me connect better with different types of people.
I listen way more than I talk now. Early on I thought my job was to present and persuade. Now I know the best thing I can do is ask the right question and then get out of the way.
I've learned to be more patient and not rush the conversation. I let the prospect set the pace instead of pushing my agenda.

questions.text: When you're in a room with a C-suite executive and a mid-level manager at the same time, how do you make sure both of them feel like you're speaking directly to them?

answers.text: I structure the conversation so I open with the big picture for the executive — what's at stake, what the outcome looks like — and then naturally bring in the operational detail that the manager cares about. I also physically make eye contact with both and use 'this affects your team directly' type language to keep everyone in the room.
I focus more on the executive since they're the decision maker, but I make sure to acknowledge the manager's concerns too.
I try to balance my messaging by addressing both levels — strategic outcomes for the executive and practical details for the manager. I make sure neither feels ignored.

questions.text: Have you ever been in a situation where you could tell a prospect wasn't buying what you were saying, even though they weren't saying it out loud? What did you do?

answers.text: Yes, I've noticed it through body language and short answers. When I sense it, I stop what I'm doing, acknowledge the room, and ask an open question to get them talking again.
I've been in that situation. I usually try to slow down, ask a question, and see if I can figure out what's bothering them.
Yes, and I've learned to just name it. I'll say something like 'I get the sense something I said isn't landing right — what am I missing?' It feels risky but it always moves the conversation forward.

questions.text: You've had a tough message to deliver to a prospect — maybe bad news about pricing, a delay, or a limitation in your product. How do you handle those conversations without losing the deal or the relationship?

answers.text: I prepare for these conversations by thinking through their likely reaction and having a solution or a plan ready. I'm honest about the issue and make it clear I'm on their side in figuring it out.

I'm direct and I don't drag it out. I lead with the issue, explain the context honestly, and come prepared with how we're going to work through it together. Prospects respect honesty a lot more than spin.
I try to soften the news by surrounding it with positives. I explain the situation and offer alternatives wherever I can.

questions.text: After years of pitching, what's the one thing you've completely stopped doing in your pitch because you realized it just doesn't work?

answers.text: I stopped trying to cover everything in one pitch. I've learned to be more focused and selective about what I present.

Leading with the company history and background. Nobody cares. I used to spend the first five minutes on 'who we are' — now I open with their problem and we get into the real conversation immediately.
I stopped using slides as a crutch. I used to hide behind a deck — now I use it as a support, not the main event.

questions.text: How do you pitch differently when you know the prospect is also talking to two or three of your competitors at the same time?

answers.text: I make sure my pitch is sharper and more tailored than what they're probably hearing from others. I focus on differentiation and relevant proof points.
I try to present our product clearly and make sure they understand what makes us unique compared to the competition.

I shift my pitch to focus on what I know our competitors can't do as well. I also try to shape how they think about the decision — the criteria they use to evaluate — so they're naturally thinking in terms of our strengths.

questions.text: Walk me through how you'd pitch to a company that's never bought a solution like yours before — they don't fully understand the problem yet, let alone the solution.

answers.text: I'd take my time to explain our product carefully and use simple language so they can understand what we do and why it would help them.
First, I'd educate them on the problem — not the solution. I'd help them see what's costing them by not having it. Once they feel the pain clearly, the solution conversation becomes a lot easier.
I'd start simple. Explain what the problem is, why it matters, and how we solve it. I wouldn't assume any prior knowledge and would check in regularly to make sure they're following.

questions.text: When you're pitching to a group of people who all have different priorities — finance wants cost savings, IT wants ease of integration, and the business owner wants speed — how do you structure your pitch so it works for all of them?

answers.text: I build my pitch around the common goal they all share and then weave in how we deliver for each person's priority specifically. I try not to make it feel like I'm switching audiences — it should feel like one story that happens to be relevant to everyone in the room.

I open with the overarching business outcome and then address each stakeholder's specific concern as I go. I make sure the pitch flows naturally and doesn't feel like three different presentations stitched together.
I address each priority one by one so everyone feels heard. I make sure finance, IT, and the business owner each get a section of the pitch that speaks to what they care about.

questions.text: With 10+ years of experience, what's your honest take on cold calling — does it still work, and how has your approach to it changed over the years?

answers.text: Cold calling is harder now but I still believe in it. I've had to adapt my approach as buyers have become more resistant to unsolicited calls.
It works — but not the way it used to. I spend more time researching before I dial now. One well-prepared call beats ten random ones every time.
Cold calling still has a place but it has to be combined with other channels. I use it as part of a bigger outreach strategy rather than the only tool.

questions.text: What's the best opening line or approach you've found that actually gets a cold call past the first 20 seconds without the prospect hanging up or shutting you down?

answers.text: I keep it short and get to the point quickly. I tell them who I am, why I'm calling, and ask if it's relevant to them — all in about 15 seconds.
I try to be friendly and engaging right away. A good tone and a clear introduction usually gets me a fair hearing.

I reference something specific and real about their business in the first sentence. Not generic — something I actually researched. It shows I'm not just dialing a list and they give me a few more seconds.

questions.text: You've called someone cold, and they say 'I'm really not interested.' What do you say next — and how do you decide when to keep going versus when to let it go?

answers.text: I'll ask one question — something like 'Is it the timing or is this just not relevant to you right now?' If they engage, great. If they shut down again, I thank them and move on. I don't burn a bridge over a cold call.
I'll try to give them a quick reason why it might be worth a few more minutes of their time. If they're still not interested, I let them go.
I try to ask a quick question to understand if it's a timing issue or a fit issue. If there's any opening, I'll take it. If not, I respect their time.

questions.text: How do you prepare for a cold call today versus how you used to prepare early in your career — what's different and why?

answers.text: I used to rely on a script. Now I prepare with context — their industry, recent activity, likely pain points — and use that to guide a more natural conversation.
I do a lot more research now. I look at their website and LinkedIn before calling so the conversation feels more relevant to them.

Early on I'd just dial. Now I spend real time looking at the company, their recent news, what the person's role involves, and what problems companies like theirs usually have. The call itself is shorter but the prep is much deeper.

questions.text: Tell me about a time when a presentation you gave didn't go the way you planned. What happened, how did you handle it in the moment, and what did you change after that?

answers.text: I've had presentations go off track when the audience started asking questions I wasn't expecting. I learned to be more flexible and not stick too rigidly to my agenda.

My demo crashed mid-presentation in front of a room full of senior stakeholders. I put my laptop away, picked up a marker, and drew out the workflow on the whiteboard while asking them questions about their process. It ended up being the best conversation I'd had with that account. After that, I always have a non-tech backup ready.

I once had a key decision maker join late and miss the context I'd built up. I had to quickly summarize without losing the room. After that I started front-loading the most important points so latecomers can still follow.

questions.text: How do you keep senior executives engaged during a presentation when you can tell they're getting impatient or distracted?

answers.text: I stop and ask them something directly. Something like 'Are we spending time on the right things for you?' It snaps them back in and usually redirects the whole conversation to what they actually care about.
I try to make the presentation more engaging by asking questions and making sure I'm covering what matters to them.
I speed up and cut to the most relevant parts. I try to read the room and drop anything that isn't immediately valuable to them.

questions.text: When you're presenting to a group and someone asks a question you don't know the answer to, what do you do — especially when it's in front of other stakeholders?

answers.text: I try to answer as best I can and let them know I'll confirm the details afterwards to make sure I've given them accurate information.
I say I don't know and that I'll get them the right answer. Making something up in front of a group is the fastest way to lose credibility permanently.
I'm honest about it. I acknowledge the question, tell them I want to give them an accurate answer rather than guessing, and commit to a specific time I'll follow up.

questions.text: How do you make sure a presentation feels like a conversation rather than a one-way information dump — especially in a virtual setting?

answers.text: Virtually, I check in constantly. I watch for camera cues, use their name, pause after key points and ask what they think. Silence in a virtual setting kills engagement fast so I build in natural breaks to invite them in.
I try to involve the audience by asking questions and encouraging them to share their thoughts during the presentation.
I ask questions throughout rather than saving them for the end. I treat every slide as a conversation starter, not a monologue.

questions.text: After 10+ years, you've probably seen deals fall apart at every stage of the process. Which stage do you find most deals die at, and what do you do specifically to prevent it?

answers.text: Deals tend to fall apart when prospects lose momentum. I try to keep the energy going with regular follow-ups and by keeping them engaged throughout.

After the proposal. The prospect goes quiet and you realise you never actually confirmed there was a real decision being made. Now I confirm budget, timeline, and who signs off before I write a single word of a proposal.
Most deals I've seen die during procurement or legal. I've learned to get those teams involved earlier so there are no last-minute surprises.

questions.text: How do you personally decide when a deal is real versus when a prospect is just stringing you along — and what do you do when you realize it's the latter?

answers.text: I watch how responsive they are and whether they're willing to move things forward. If they keep pushing things back without a good reason, I start to question it.
Usually my gut tells me something is off. I'll ask a few direct questions to test how serious they are and decide whether to keep investing time.

I look for commitment — real commitment. Are they showing up to meetings? Are they sharing internal information? Are they introducing me to other people in the business? If it's all talk and no action, I ask them directly where this is really going.

questions.text: Walk me through how you manage a deal that's been in your pipeline for way too long — what steps do you take to either move it forward or cut it loose?

answers.text: I try to re-engage them with something new — a relevant case study, a product update, anything that gives me a reason to reach out and get the conversation going again.

I reassess the deal — is the pain still real, is there budget, has anything changed internally? Then I either find a new angle to re-engage or I have an honest conversation about whether the timing is right.

I call it out. I have a direct conversation where I tell them I want to make sure I'm being useful to them and ask honestly if this is still something they're planning to move on. Most of the time that conversation either unlocks it or ends it — both are better than it just sitting there.

questions.text: How do you balance working multiple complex deals at the same time without anything slipping through the cracks?

answers.text: I use a combination of my calendar, CRM, and personal notes to keep track of where each deal is and what I need to do next.
My CRM is my brain for this. Every deal has a next step with a date attached. If a deal doesn't have a next step, it's not a real deal.
I prioritize deals by stage and potential value, and I block time in my week specifically for each one. I also keep detailed notes after every interaction so I can pick up exactly where I left off.

questions.text: What's the one question you've learned to always ask early in a sales conversation that tells you whether this deal is worth your time?

answers.text: I usually ask about their budget and what they're trying to solve. Those two things tell me quickly whether it's worth pursuing.
I ask about their timeline and what's prompting them to explore solutions now. The answer tells me a lot about how serious they are.
I ask some version of 'What's driving you to look at this now?' If they can't answer that clearly, there's no urgency and no real deal.

questions.text: How do you get a prospect to open up and share information they're not immediately willing to share — like budget, internal politics, or who else is involved in the decision?

answers.text: I share first. I'll say something like 'Other companies we work with in your space usually have a budget in the range of X — does that feel close to where you're thinking?' It lowers their guard because I've given something before asking for something.
I ask indirectly. Instead of 'what's your budget?' I ask 'how do you typically approach investments like this?' It gets me the same information without feeling intrusive.
I build rapport first and make them feel comfortable before I go to the harder questions. Once there's trust, people share more.

questions.text: Have you ever asked a question in a sales conversation that completely changed the direction of the deal — in a good or bad way? What was it, and what did you learn?

answers.text: I've had questions that opened up new angles I hadn't considered. It taught me that the right question at the right time can completely change where a conversation goes.
Yes. I once asked who else needed to be involved in the decision and found out there was a whole team I didn't know about. It reset the timeline but saved us from a nasty surprise later on.

I asked a CFO 'What happens to your business if this problem isn't solved in the next 12 months?' He went quiet, then said 'honestly, we'd probably lose two of our biggest clients.' That one question made the whole deal move faster than anything I'd said before.

questions.text: How do you handle it when a prospect gives you very short, surface-level answers and doesn't want to go deep? How do you draw more out of them without making it feel like an interrogation?

answers.text: I change my approach — less direct questions, more conversational statements that invite a response. Something like 'I've seen a lot of companies in your space struggle with X' usually gets them talking.

I slow down and share something myself — a relevant observation or a challenge I've seen at similar companies. It usually prompts them to respond with their own perspective. People open up when you go first.
I try different types of questions and give them space to answer. If they're guarded, I try not to push too hard and let the conversation build naturally.

questions.text: Have you ever gotten deep into a deal only to realize you were talking to the wrong person the whole time? How did you discover that, and how did you recover?

answers.text: I've been there. I found out when the proposal went nowhere because my contact had no influence over the budget. I had to find a different way in — through a referral from someone they respected.

Yes — and it's one of the most expensive lessons in sales. I discovered it when my contact couldn't get a meeting with their own leadership to discuss what we'd been working on for months. I had to restart the relationship at a higher level, which I should have done from the beginning. Now I always ask early who else will be involved and I try to meet them before the deal gets too far.
It's happened. When I realised it, I asked my contact to help me get access to the right people. Sometimes they help, sometimes they don't.

questions.text: When a deal suddenly goes quiet after things were moving along well, what do you think is usually happening on the prospect's side — and how do you find out for sure?

answers.text: I follow up to see what's going on. Sometimes it's just that they've been busy and the deal picks back up. Other times something has changed and I need to figure out what.

Something changed internally — priorities shifted, budget got cut, or someone left. I reach out and say it directly: 'Things went quiet and I want to make sure I'm not missing something — what's changed?' It works almost every time.
Usually it's an internal issue — budget freeze, change in priorities, or someone getting cold feet. I reach out with something of value and use it as a reason to check in.

questions.text: How do you figure out the real buying process in a company — not just what they tell you, but who actually has influence, who signs off, and what's really driving the timeline?

answers.text: I ask my main contact to walk me through the last time they made a similar decision — who was involved, how long it took, what almost stopped it. That story tells me everything I need to know about how things actually work there.
I ask questions throughout the process to understand who else is involved and what the approval process looks like.
I ask directly about the decision process early on — who's involved, what the steps are, what could slow it down. Then I validate it as the deal progresses.

questions.text: Tell me about a time you lost a deal not because of price or product, but because of something happening internally at the prospect's company. How did you handle it, and what would you do differently?

answers.text: It's happened — things outside my control derailed a deal I thought was in good shape. I try to stay connected and keep the door open for when the timing is better.

Lost a deal six months in because the champion got promoted and the new person came with their own vendor relationships. I handled it by staying in contact with my original champion in their new role. The lesson — always build more than one relationship inside an account so the deal doesn't live or die on one person.
I had a deal fall apart because of a company restructure that changed the budget ownership. There wasn't much I could do at that point. I kept the relationship warm and came back six months later.

questions.text: What's the toughest objection you regularly face in your deals, and after all these years, what's the most effective way you've found to handle it?

answers.text: Price objections are common. I handle them by reinforcing the value and ROI so the conversation shifts from cost to investment.

The toughest is 'we're happy with what we have.' It's tough because there's no obvious pain to solve. I handle it by asking questions about what 'happy' actually looks like and where the gaps are — because there are always gaps.
'It's too expensive' is one I face a lot. I've gotten better at reframing it around what it costs them not to solve the problem rather than defending our price.

questions.text: How do you tell the difference between a prospect who has a real concern versus one who's just not interested but doesn't want to say it directly?

answers.text: Real objections come with detail. When someone says 'your pricing is higher than expected' and can tell me what they expected, that's real. When they say 'it's just not the right time' without any specifics, that's a polite no. I've learned to just ask: 'Is this a concern you want us to work through or are you telling me this isn't the right fit?'
Experience helps you read these situations. I've learned to ask follow-up questions to see if they're genuinely interested in resolving the concern.
If the objection is specific and they engage when I respond, it's real. If they stay vague and keep deflecting, it's usually not going anywhere.

questions.text: Have you ever had a prospect raise an objection very late in the deal — almost at the finish line — that nearly killed it? How did you handle it?

answers.text: Late objections usually mean something wasn't uncovered early enough. I stay calm, take it seriously, and work through it — but I've also learned to ask broader questions earlier so these surprises are less common.
It's happened. I try to address it quickly and bring in whoever from our side can help resolve it. Late objections are stressful but they can usually be worked through.

Yes. Security concerns from a technical team that had never been involved before. I was frustrated but I didn't show it. I brought in our technical team, addressed every concern in writing, and scheduled a dedicated session to walk them through it. It delayed the close by three weeks but we got there.

questions.text: When a prospect says your price is too high, how do you respond — and how has that response evolved over your years in sales?

answers.text: I don't rush to justify the price. I try to understand what they're comparing us to and then refocus on the value we bring relative to that benchmark.
I explain the value in more detail and show them how the ROI justifies the investment. I've gotten much better at making that case convincingly over the years.
Early in my career I'd get defensive or start offering discounts. Now I get curious. I ask 'compared to what?' and let that answer guide the whole conversation. The issue is rarely the price itself.

questions.text: How do you explain the value of what you sell in a way that doesn't sound like every other sales pitch the prospect has already heard?

answers.text: I skip the corporate positioning and get straight to the specific outcome they're going to get. Real numbers, real results from real customers they can relate to.
I focus on what makes us different and use customer stories to make the value feel real rather than just theoretical.

I use their language, not mine. I base my value statement on what they told me their problem is. If it sounds like their problem coming back to them as a solution, it doesn't sound like a pitch at all.

questions.text: Have you ever been in a situation where the prospect could see your product was good but still didn't see why it was worth the price? How did you bridge that gap?

answers.text: I brought in a customer reference at a similar company so they could hear directly what the impact had been. Sometimes that third-party voice closes the gap faster than anything I say.
I walked them through the ROI in more detail and showed them how it would pay for itself over time.

I shifted the conversation from the product to the problem. We built out a simple calculation together — what this issue is currently costing them. Once they saw the number, our price looked very different.

questions.text: When you're selling to someone who's very numbers-driven and wants to see a clear ROI before they commit, how do you build that case — especially when you don't have all their internal data?

answers.text: I put together a high-level ROI model based on what I know about their business and similar companies, and I present it as a starting point for discussion.

I ask them to help me build it. 'I don't have your exact numbers but you do — let's work through this together.' They end up owning the ROI model and it's much more credible than anything I could have produced on my own.
I use industry benchmarks and data from similar customers as proxies and then ask them to validate the assumptions. It gives the model credibility even without their exact numbers.

questions.text: How do you adjust the value story you tell depending on who you're talking to — for example, the difference between talking to a CFO versus someone in operations?

answers.text: Same product, completely different story. With a CFO it's about risk, return, and financial impact. With operations it's about time, effort, and day-to-day pain relief. I know the product well enough to tell it either way.
I think about what each person cares about and make sure I'm speaking to that. A CFO wants numbers and a manager wants to know how it helps their team.
I adjust the emphasis — financial metrics and ROI for the CFO, practical outcomes and efficiency gains for operations. The core message is the same but the angle changes.

questions.text: After 10+ years of selling, how has your sense of who your ideal customer really is changed — and what experiences shaped that?

answers.text: I've refined it significantly. Early on I chased anything. Now I know exactly what profile of company and what type of buyer gives us the best chance of success — and I'm disciplined about it.

I used to think bigger was always better. I've learned that the best customers aren't necessarily the biggest ones — they're the ones who feel the problem acutely, are ready to change, and have someone internally who owns the outcome. A few bad fits taught me that faster than any win.
Over the years I've got a much clearer picture of who's a good fit and who isn't. Experience just gives you better instincts for it.

questions.text: How quickly can you tell in the first conversation whether a prospect is a good fit or not — and what are the specific signals you look for?

answers.text: Pretty quickly now. I'm listening for whether the pain is real and urgent, whether they've tried to solve it before, and whether the person I'm talking to has any stake in fixing it. Those three things tell me almost everything.
I can usually get a feel for it in the first call based on how they respond to questions and how engaged they are in the conversation.
Usually within the first meeting. I look at how specific they are about their problem, how senior the person is, and whether they're actually exploring solutions or just gathering information.

questions.text: Have you ever chased a deal that looked great on paper but turned out to be a bad fit? What happened, and what did you learn from it?

answers.text: It's happened. You learn from those experiences to ask more questions upfront before getting too invested in a deal.

Yes. The numbers looked right but their internal culture wasn't a good match for how we work. It dragged on, eventually fell apart, and cost a lot of time. Now I pay attention to culture fit as well as commercial fit.

Big logo, big budget, ticked every box on the surface. Spent four months on it. When we finally got deep into their requirements, they needed customisation we couldn't deliver. I should have asked harder questions in week one. Now I qualify for fit aggressively, not just for revenue potential.

questions.text: How do you personally decide to walk away from a prospect who doesn't fit your ideal profile but is very interested in buying from you?

answers.text: I think about what happens after the sale. If I can't see them being a successful customer, I'm setting both of us up for a painful relationship. I'd rather have that honest conversation now than deal with a bad customer for the next two years.
It's a hard call. I weigh up the revenue opportunity against the risk of a bad customer experience. If the fit is genuinely poor, I'll have an honest conversation rather than force it.
I try to flag the concerns and see if there's a way to make it work. If there isn't, I'll let them know honestly.

questions.text: What's your personal follow-up strategy after a first meeting — what do you do, when do you do it, and why does that approach work for you?

answers.text: I follow up within a day or two with a thank you and a summary of what we discussed along with the next steps we agreed on.
Same day, short email. I recap what they said — not what I said — and confirm the next step we agreed on. It shows I was listening and keeps momentum going before they get busy with the next thing.

I send a follow-up within 24 hours that summarises the key points, confirms next steps, and includes something relevant — a case study, an article, something that adds value beyond just 'thanks for your time.'

questions.text: How many times do you follow up with a prospect who hasn't responded before you decide to move on — and how do you make each follow-up feel different so it doesn't seem like you're just checking in?

answers.text: I follow up several times, trying to vary my approach between email, phone, and LinkedIn so I'm not just sending the same message over and over.

I follow up until I get a response — yes, no, or not now. But each follow-up needs to give them a reason to reply. A new insight, a relevant story, a question they haven't been asked before. 'Just checking in' is the laziest thing in sales.
I usually go to six or seven touches before stepping back. Each one tries to add something new — a different angle, a different medium, or a different piece of value so it doesn't feel repetitive.

questions.text: What's the most creative or effective follow-up you've done that got a response from a prospect who had gone completely quiet?

answers.text: I sent a handwritten note once with a relevant article attached. In a world of emails it stood out completely and restarted a conversation I thought was dead.

I sent a very brief, honest message saying I didn't want to keep bothering them but wanted to know if the timing was just off or if they'd moved in a different direction. That honesty usually gets a reply.
A short video. Thirty seconds, no script, just me talking about something relevant I'd seen in their industry that week. It felt personal in a way email never does. Got a response within an hour.

questions.text: How do you stay on a prospect's radar over a long sales cycle — sometimes six months or more — without coming across as pushy or desperate?

answers.text: Value-add only. I share things that are genuinely useful to them — industry news, a relevant event, an introduction to someone they should know. If every touchpoint gives them something, it doesn't feel like pestering.
I keep in touch regularly but try not to be too salesy about it. I share relevant content and check in periodically without always pushing for an update on the deal.
I map out the touchpoints over the cycle and make sure each one has a genuine reason behind it. I avoid any message that's just about where the deal stands — it always has to be about them.

questions.text: Walk me through exactly how you prepare for an important sales call — what do you research, what do you plan, and how long does it take you?

answers.text: I research the company and the people I'm meeting, prepare my agenda and key talking points, and make sure I know what outcome I'm aiming for.

I look at the company website, recent press, their LinkedIn and the people I'll be meeting. I prepare my key questions, anticipate likely objections, and set a clear goal for the call. Usually takes me 30-45 minutes for a high-priority meeting.

I research the company and the individual. For the company — recent news, their business model, industry challenges. For the person — their LinkedIn, how long they've been in the role, anything they've written or said publicly. Then I write down the three things I need to find out on the call and the one outcome I want by the end. That's it. The rest is listening.

questions.text: What's the minimum you need to know about a prospect before you feel ready to get on a call with them — and what happens when you can't find that information?

answers.text: What they do, who they serve, and roughly what pain they're likely carrying based on their role. If I can't find it, I build my opening questions around discovering it. A good discovery question beats a wrong assumption every time.
I like to know the basics about their company and role before the call. If I can't find it, I do my best with what I have and ask more questions on the call.

I need to understand their business model, their role, and their likely challenges at minimum. If I can't find it, I'm upfront on the call — I tell them I haven't been able to find much and ask if they can give me some context.

questions.text: How do you set the agenda for a sales call in a way that keeps you in control of the conversation but still makes the prospect feel like it's their meeting?

answers.text: I share a light agenda at the start and frame it around what we want them to get out of the meeting, not what I want to cover. Then I confirm they're comfortable with it before we start.
I set an agenda and share it at the start of the call. I make sure to ask if there's anything they want to add or change before we get going.

I open by suggesting an agenda and then asking them if that works or if there's something they want to prioritise. They almost always say it's fine, but asking gives them ownership of it. And I always build in time for their questions at the front — not just at the end.

questions.text: Tell me about a call you went into well-prepared and it still went sideways. What happened, how did you handle it, and what did you do differently next time?

answers.text: The prospect had done their own research and came in with very specific technical questions I wasn't prepared to answer in detail. I handled it by being honest about what I knew and what I'd need to confirm, and I brought in a technical resource for the next call.

Prepared for a CFO conversation. Showed up and found out she'd brought their legal team and IT director. Completely different conversation. I put my prep aside, asked everyone what they were hoping to get out of the meeting, and let that guide it. Wasn't perfect but it was better than pretending they weren't in the room.
Unexpected things happen on calls. I've learned to stay flexible and not get thrown off when the conversation doesn't go the way I planned.

questions.text: When a prospect pushes hard for a discount, how do you decide whether to hold your price or give something — and what does your thought process look like in that moment?

answers.text: I assess how serious the pressure is and whether they're genuinely budget-constrained or just testing. Then I decide what I'm comfortable offering within my authority.
I don't move on price unless I get something back — a longer commitment, a quicker close, a reference. I never give something for nothing in a negotiation.

I ask myself: is this a price issue or a value issue? If I haven't made the value clear enough, a discount won't fix the real problem. I'd rather go back to the value conversation than cut the price and lose their respect.

questions.text: Tell me about the toughest negotiation you've been in as an individual seller. What made it hard, and how did you get to a deal — or did you walk away?

answers.text: I've been in some tough negotiations over the years. The hardest are when both sides are far apart on price. You have to be patient and find what the other side really needs to feel good about the deal.

Procurement came in at the last minute with a list of demands that would have made the deal unprofitable. What made it hard was my own pressure to close. I took a day to reset, went back with a clear line on what we could and couldn't do, and explained why. They pushed back once more and I held firm. We got to a deal that worked for both sides — not perfect for either of us, but fair.

A deal where the prospect went back to market midway through negotiation to get competitive quotes. I had to hold my value position while managing the risk of losing it entirely. I stayed confident, brought in some additional proof points, and we closed without a major concession.

questions.text: How do you negotiate when you know the prospect has other options and genuinely doesn't need to choose you — what's your strategy when you're not the only one in the room?

answers.text: I focus on what makes us the lower-risk choice. Features and price are easy to compare — implementation support, account management, and track record with similar companies are harder to quantify and that's where I try to win.

I stop competing on price and start competing on relationship and risk. I ask them what would make this an easy decision and then focus on whatever that is. Usually it's not price — it's confidence, trust, or a specific capability they're worried about.
I emphasise our strengths and what differentiates us. If there are other options on the table, I make sure they have a clear reason to choose us.

questions.text: Have you ever made a concession in a negotiation that you later regretted? What was it, and what would you do differently now?

answers.text: I once agreed to a payment structure that created ongoing admin problems for our team. I was so focused on closing the commercial terms that I didn't think through the operational impact. Now I think about what happens after the signature, not just during the negotiation.

Gave a significant discount under end-of-quarter pressure. The deal was going to close anyway — I just didn't know it yet. I panicked and gave away margin I didn't need to. Now I remind myself that urgency is usually mine, not theirs.
Yes. I gave a discount that I didn't need to give and it affected my overall performance for the quarter. I've learned to hold firmer and trust the value more.

questions.text: How do you go about truly understanding a prospect's business — beyond just what they tell you in a sales meeting — so you can speak to their real challenges?

answers.text: I research their company thoroughly and ask good discovery questions so I understand their business from multiple angles, not just what they initially tell me.

I read their annual report, listen to earnings calls if they're public, look at their customer reviews, and talk to people in their industry before I ever get in front of them. By the time we meet, I should know more about their competitive pressures than most of their own team.

I do my homework before every meeting. Company news, industry reports, their social media, LinkedIn activity of their leadership team. I also ask better questions once I'm in the room — things that go beyond the surface level.

questions.text: Have you ever surprised a prospect by knowing something about their business or industry that they didn't expect you to know? How did that change the dynamic of the conversation?

answers.text: A few times. I mentioned a competitor move they weren't aware of and it got their attention immediately. It showed I was across their market and not just reading from a generic script.

Yes — I referenced a specific regulatory change coming in their industry that they hadn't thought about in the context of our conversation. The whole meeting shifted. They stopped seeing me as a vendor and started treating me like someone who actually understood their world.
It's happened and it always creates a good impression. When you know their business well it builds credibility quickly.

questions.text: When a prospect tells you what they need, how do you figure out if that's actually what they need — or if there's something deeper going on that they haven't told you yet?

answers.text: I ask why they need it. And then I ask why again. Usually the third or fourth layer of the answer is where the real problem lives. What people ask for and what they actually need are often very different things.
I ask follow-up questions to make sure I understand the full picture and not just the surface-level requirement.
I dig into the context behind the request. 'What's driven this to be a priority now?' and 'What have you already tried?' usually reveal a lot more than the initial ask.

questions.text: How do you keep up with what's happening in your customers' industries so your conversations always feel relevant and current — not generic?

answers.text: I follow industry news, set up alerts for key topics, and read relevant content regularly so I'm not walking into conversations without knowing what's going on in their world.

I treat industry knowledge as part of my job, not a bonus. I follow the same publications my customers read, go to the same events, and track the same trends. When I talk to them, it should feel like talking to a peer, not a salesperson.

I have a morning habit — fifteen minutes on industry news, analyst updates, and LinkedIn for my top accounts. It's not glamorous but it means I always have something relevant to bring to every conversation.

questions.text: How do you find out which competitors a prospect is talking to — and once you know, how does that change your approach?

answers.text: I try to find out through questions and by reading the signals in the conversation. Knowing who else is involved helps me tailor my approach.

I just ask — early and directly. 'Are you talking to anyone else?' Most people will tell you. Once I know, I adjust where I spend time in the conversation to make sure our strengths against that specific competitor are clear without me ever needing to mention them by name.
I ask directly and I also pick up clues from the questions they ask — certain questions tell you exactly who else is in the picture. Once I know, I sharpen my differentiation accordingly.

questions.text: Tell me about a deal where you went up against a stronger or more well-known competitor. What was your strategy, and how did it play out?

answers.text: I focused on our strengths and made sure the prospect understood why we were the better fit for their specific situation, even if the competitor had a bigger name.

I've faced bigger competitors often. My strategy is always to find the gap — what they're bad at or where they're a poor fit for this specific prospect — and make that the story. I don't try to beat them head-on.

I was up against a market leader with a bigger brand and a bigger budget. I stopped competing on their terms and found the thing they couldn't do well — their implementation was notoriously slow. I made speed and hands-on support the whole story. We won because I made the decision about the thing they cared about most, not the thing that looked good on a comparison sheet.

questions.text: When a prospect brings up something a competitor does better than you, how do you handle that conversation honestly without losing ground?

answers.text: I don't dismiss it. I acknowledge the strength, then reframe the conversation around the broader picture — what they're optimising for overall, not just one feature or capability.

I agree with them if it's true. Nothing builds more trust in a sales conversation than acknowledging a competitor does something well. Then I redirect to what matters most for their situation and where we win.
I try not to get defensive. I acknowledge their point and then make sure they have the full picture of what we bring to the table.

questions.text: How do you stay up to date on what your competitors are doing — their pricing, their pitches, their product changes — without crossing any ethical lines?

answers.text: I use public sources consistently — their marketing, review sites, industry reports, and what I hear directly from prospects who are also talking to them. I also pay attention to the questions prospects ask me, which often reflect what competitors have been saying.
I follow their public activity — website updates, press releases, social media — and pay attention to what prospects mention about them during conversations.

Everything is public if you know where to look. Their website, their job postings, customer reviews on G2 or Capterra, what their sales reps say on LinkedIn, what prospects tell me in discovery. You don't need to cross any lines — the information is everywhere.
